interactions.label: What distinguishes the primary complex of childhood tuberculosis from typical ad

params.question: What distinguishes the primary complex of childhood tuberculosis from typical adult pulmonary TB?

answers.text: Hilar lymph node enlargement is disproportionately prominent compared to the parenchymal lesion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The Ghon focus itself is small (1–2 cm), but the draining hilar lymph nodes enlarge markedly in children, producing airway compression — a feature rarely seen in adult cavitary disease.

answers.text: Children develop large cavitary lung lesions earlier than adults

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cavitary disease is characteristic of adult reactivation TB. In children, the immature immune response produces prominent lymph node enlargement rather than lung cavities.

answers.text: The Ghon focus in children forms in the upper lobes rather than the lower

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Inhaled bacilli settle in the mid and lower lung zones where ventilation is greatest. Upper-lobe predilection is a feature of adult reactivation TB, not childhood primary infection.

answers.text: Children shed more bacilli in sputum than adults, making diagnosis easier

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Childhood TB is characteristically paucibacillary — children produce far fewer organisms in sputum than adults, which is precisely why microbiological diagnosis is more difficult in this age group.

overallFeedback.feedback: In childhood TB, the primary complex is dominated by hilar lymph node enlargement rather than lung parenchymal destruction. This lymph-node-centric pattern explains why airway compression, not cavitation, is the characteristic paediatric complication.

Correct. The hallmark of the childhood primary complex is disproportionate hilar lymph node enlargement, which can compress airways and cause segmental collapse — unlike adult TB where cavitary lung destruction predominates.

interactions.label: A 2-year-old with pulmonary tuberculosis develops segmental lung collapse on che

params.question: A 2-year-old with pulmonary tuberculosis develops segmental lung collapse on chest X-ray. Which mechanism of childhood TB complications BEST explains this finding?

answers.text: Direct destruction of lung parenchyma by caseating granulomas

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Granulomatous tissue destruction causes localised caseous necrosis, not the pattern of segmental collapse. The collapse points to airway obstruction from an external compressive force.

answers.text: Compression of the bronchus by enlarged hilar lymph nodes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Enlarged hilar lymph nodes can compress an adjacent bronchus, obstructing airflow and producing the classic segmental or lobar collapse seen on imaging — the so-called 'peanut-shaped' collapse.

answers.text: Haematogenous dissemination of bacilli to the lung periphery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Haematogenous spread produces widespread miliary nodules across both lungs, not focal segmental collapse. The collapse pattern is caused by localised airway obstruction from lymph node pressure.

answers.text: Immune-mediated damage to the alveolar capillary membrane

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Alveolar capillary damage is not a recognised mechanism of TB complications in children. The three mechanisms are direct tissue destruction, pressure effects from lymph nodes, and haematogenous dissemination.

overallFeedback.feedback: Segmental lung collapse in childhood TB results from enlarged hilar lymph nodes pressing on an adjacent bronchus. This pressure effect is one of three complication mechanisms: direct tissue destruction, pressure from lymph nodes, and haematogenous dissemination.

Correct. In childhood TB, the hilar lymph nodes enlarge much more than in adults, and they can compress adjacent bronchi — producing segmental collapse. This pressure-effect mechanism is uniquely prominent in children because their airways are narrower.

interactions.label: A child with suspected pulmonary TB has a NEGATIVE CBNAAT result on gastric aspi

params.question: A child with suspected pulmonary TB has a NEGATIVE CBNAAT result on gastric aspirate, but clinical features and chest X-ray findings remain strongly suggestive. What is the MOST appropriate next step?

answers.text: Rule out tuberculosis and investigate alternative diagnoses

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A negative CBNAAT does not exclude TB in children. Sensitivity on gastric aspirate is only 70–80 %, well below the 95 % seen in smear-positive adults. Clinical and radiological evidence must be weighed alongside molecular results.

answers.text: Repeat the same CBNAAT test on a fresh gastric aspirate sample

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Simply repeating the same test offers limited additional yield in paucibacillary paediatric specimens. When CBNAAT is negative but suspicion is high, the recommended escalation is BACTEC MGIT liquid culture, which has higher sensitivity.

answers.text: Escalate to BACTEC MGIT liquid culture while continuing clinical evaluation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: BACTEC MGIT liquid culture has higher sensitivity than CBNAAT for low-burden paediatric specimens, though results take 1–3 weeks. It is the recommended next step when rapid molecular testing is negative but clinical suspicion persists.

MDR-TB treatment requires evidence of drug resistance. A negative CBNAAT means MTB DNA was not detected at all — it provides no information about resistance patterns. The appropriate step is culture-based confirmation.

overallFeedback.feedback: In children, CBNAAT sensitivity on gastric aspirate is only 70–80 %. When the result is negative but clinical suspicion remains high, BACTEC MGIT liquid culture is the recommended next step — it has higher sensitivity, though results take 1–3 weeks rather than hours.

Correct. CBNAAT sensitivity on paediatric gastric aspirate is only 70–80 %, so a negative result cannot exclude TB when clinical and radiological evidence is compelling. BACTEC MGIT liquid culture, with its higher sensitivity, is the appropriate next investigation.

interactions.label: Pyrazinamide is essential during the intensive phase of anti-TB treatment specif

params.question: Pyrazinamide is essential during the intensive phase of anti-TB treatment specifically because it targets:

answers.text: Rapidly multiplying extracellular bacilli in aerated lung cavities

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rapidly dividing extracellular bacilli are the primary targets of isoniazid and rifampicin. Pyrazinamide's unique contribution is reaching the bacterial sub-population that these drugs cannot eliminate effectively.

answers.text: Dormant persister bacilli within the acidic environment of macrophages

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pyrazinamide is uniquely active at the acidic pH inside macrophage phagosomes, exactly where dormant persister bacilli survive with low metabolic activity. This is why it is given only during the intensive phase — to clear persisters early.
Cell-wall-deficient L-forms are not the target of standard anti-TB drugs. Pyrazinamide acts specifically on persister bacilli sheltering within the acidic intracellular compartments of macrophages.

answers.text: Drug-resistant mutant bacilli in caseous necrotic tissue

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Preventing resistance is the role of the multi-drug regimen as a whole, not pyrazinamide alone. Pyrazinamide's specific contribution is targeting dormant persisters in the acidic macrophage environment that other drugs cannot reach.

overallFeedback.feedback: Inside a TB lesion, different bacterial sub-populations behave differently. Pyrazinamide's unique role is killing dormant persister bacilli that hide within the acidic environment of macrophage phagosomes — a niche that isoniazid and rifampicin cannot penetrate effectively.

Correct. Each first-line drug is matched to a specific bacterial sub-population. Pyrazinamide is uniquely active in the acidic pH inside macrophages, where dormant persister bacilli survive — making it indispensable during the intensive phase.

interactions.label: BCG vaccination given at birth provides reliable protection against pulmonary tu

params.question: BCG vaccination given at birth provides reliable protection against pulmonary tuberculosis throughout childhood.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: BCG's strongest benefit is approximately 80 % protection against severe forms — miliary TB and tuberculous meningitis. However, its protection against pulmonary TB is far less reliable and diminishes with age, which is why a BCG scar should never be used to rule out pulmonary TB in a symptomatic child.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Well done. BCG provides approximately 80 % protection against the most severe disseminated forms — miliary TB and tuberculous meningitis — but its protection against ordinary pulmonary TB is limited and wanes over the years. That is why contact history remains the single most important screening step.
